name: Disable Fullscreen Optimizations
what: Turns off Windows' hybrid fullscreen compositor for a specific game's .exe.
why: Genuinely changes frame pacing / latency in SOME games and hurts others — it's per-game, so measure it. Not a global win.

name: Windows Game Mode
what: Prioritizes the foreground game for CPU/GPU scheduling and holds back background interruptions.
why: Modest, low-risk benefit on most rigs; larger on busy/background-heavy systems. Compy can toggle it for you. One catch: game-recording software (AMD ReLive, NVIDIA ShadowPlay / Instant Replay) often resets Game Mode to off at every login, so it can refuse to stay on after a restart — that's the recording app, not the toggle.

name: MSI Mode (Message-Signaled Interrupts)
what: Switches a device from a shared legacy line IRQ to dedicated message-signaled interrupts.
why: A real interrupt-latency win on a device that actually benefits (GPU / NIC / NVMe), though blanket-forcing it everywhere is negligible on modern setups — driver-dependent and reversible. Compy surfaces it as advisory, never forces it.

name: Force HPET / useplatformclock
what: Forces Windows to use the High Precision Event Timer via a boot flag.
why: Refused. On modern Windows this almost always RAISES latency and causes stutter — the OS already picks the best timer. A classic forum tweak that backfires.

name: Disable Core Isolation / VBS
what: Turns off virtualization-based security / memory integrity, which can cost CPU performance.
why: Real performance gain, real security cost — it removes a kernel exploit mitigation. The gain is genuine: often a few percent, and more in some CPU-bound games depending on your chip — but you're trading away a real protection for it, so Compy shows it as a trade-off you decide, never auto-applied.

name: Random registry "FPS boost" hacks
what: Assorted forum / video registry edits promising free FPS.
why: Almost all are placebo or actively harmful — undocumented keys, no measurable effect, easy to break settings. Compy refuses the lot.

name: XMP / EXPO memory profile
what: Enables your RAM's rated speed profile in BIOS (it runs slower out of the box).
why: The #1 low-risk BIOS win — real gains in CPU-bound games and 1% lows. If the PC fails to boot, clear CMOS and it's back; run a memory stability test after enabling.

name: Resizable BAR / Smart Access Memory
what: Lets the CPU access the GPU's whole VRAM in one mapping instead of small chunks (BIOS + driver).
why: Real but title-dependent — a few percent in many games, big in a handful, slightly negative in rare ones. Enable it, measure, and disable per-title only if a game regresses.

name: Custom fan curves / better cooling
what: Tunes case/GPU/CPU fan response so parts stay cooler under load.
why: One of the safest 'performance' tweaks there is: modern parts boost higher when cooler, so a sane curve buys free sustained clocks. No registry to edit — the one real trade-off is fan noise, since a more aggressive curve spins up louder, so it is a comfort-vs-cooling balance you set to taste.

name: NVIDIA Reflex
what: In-game toggle that syncs rendering to input to genuinely cut click-to-display latency.
why: The real latency win on NVIDIA — turn it on wherever a game offers it. (With Reflex on, leave the driver's Low Latency Mode off; they conflict.)

name: Low Latency Mode (driver setting)
what: Driver-level cap on how many frames the CPU queues ahead of the GPU.
why: Real but conditional: 'On' is a good default, 'Ultra' only helps when you are GPU-bound (the GPU pegged near 100%) — and turn it OFF in games with Reflex / Anti-Lag 2 integration, which supersede it.

name: AMD Anti-Lag+ (old driver-level version)
what: AMD's old driver-injected latency reducer (distinct from in-game Anti-Lag 2).
why: The cautionary tale: it injected into game code and got players VAC-banned in CS2. Use in-game Anti-Lag 2 instead — never a driver-injected hack in an anti-cheat game.

name: VRR + V-Sync + frame cap (the sync stack)
what: VRR on, V-Sync on in the driver, and an FPS cap a few frames below refresh.
why: The most felt improvement available on a VRR monitor: tear-free AND low-latency, because the cap keeps you inside the VRR window. This is where 'smooth' actually comes from.

name: FPS cap below refresh rate
what: Caps frames ~3 below your monitor's refresh (e.g. 141 on a 144 Hz panel).
why: Keeps VRR engaged, avoids V-Sync backpressure, stabilizes frametimes, and lowers heat. One of the few tweaks that's real on nearly every setup.

name: Frame Generation (DLSS FG / FSR / AFMF)
what: GPU generates extra in-between frames for higher displayed FPS.
why: Real smoothness for single-player on a high-Hz display — but it ADDS input latency. Use it in story games, never in competitive shooters. Displayed FPS is not the same as response.

name: Upscaling (DLSS / FSR / XeSS quality modes)
what: Renders at lower resolution and AI-upscales to native.
why: The rare free lunch: quality modes usually give MORE real FPS and LOWER latency than native with near-native image quality. Distinct from frame-gen (which adds latency).

name: Shader cache size (unlimited / 10 GB)
what: Lets the driver keep more compiled shaders on disk.
why: Cheap and real, but for a specific kind of stutter: a bigger cache lets the driver reuse compiled shaders instead of rebuilding them after a driver update or a cache wipe — it does not stop a game's first-run shader compile (that is the engine's job, which is why letting games finish their shader pre-compile screens matters more). The size knob is mainly an NVIDIA thing; AMD's cache has no size cap. Costs only disk space.

name: High / Ultimate Performance power plan
what: Stops Windows from downclocking/parking CPU cores at light load.
why: Real but narrower than it sounds: it mainly steadies frame pacing in CPU-bound games (and stops light-load core downclocking), with little to gain in GPU-bound ones — at the cost of idle watts. Compy can switch plans for you, with the exact previous plan recorded for rollback.

name: Disable Game Bar background recording (Game DVR)
what: Turns off Windows' always-on gameplay capture buffer.
why: Real on weaker rigs — capture overhead you may never have wanted. Harmless to disable if you don't use instant replay; Compy treats it as a safe, reversible toggle.

name: Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling (HAGS)
what: Moves GPU scheduling from the OS to the GPU itself (reboot required).
why: Helps latency and is required for some frame-gen — but occasionally regresses specific titles. Worth testing on, with a measured before/after rather than vibes.

name: Disable MPO (Multi-Plane Overlay)
what: Registry value that turns off a display compositing feature.
why: A legitimate FIX for a real flicker/stutter bug on some multi-monitor/VRR setups — but ONLY if you have the symptom. Cargo-culting it on a healthy system does nothing. Reversible.

name: Disable telemetry services (DiagTrack etc.)
what: Stops Windows' usage/diagnostics reporting services.
why: The cleanest debloat win — no effect on stability or updates. Honesty note: this is about privacy and background hygiene, not FPS. Compy offers it as a safe, reversible toggle.

name: Disable SysMain (Superfetch)
what: Stops the service that preloads frequently-used apps into RAM.
why: On an SSD/NVMe there's little to gain from preloading, so turning SysMain off cuts its background disk activity and steadies RAM use. It doesn't 'free' a set amount of memory — that cache was reclaimable standby RAM Windows already releases when apps need it. KEEP it on hard drives. Compy already gates this recommendation on your storage type.

name: Disabling startup apps
what: Stops vendor bloat (RGB suites, updaters) from launching at boot.
why: The biggest FELT win in all of debloating — faster boots, fewer background stutter sources. Safe: disabling startup doesn't uninstall anything.

name: Disable Windows Search indexing
what: Stops the file indexer service.
why: Near-zero on SSD/NVMe (the common case) and it breaks instant Start-menu search. Only old HDD systems see real relief — which is exactly the only case Compy suggests it.

name: Visual effects → best performance
what: Disables Windows UI animations and effects.
why: Snappier-feeling DESKTOP, not more FPS in games — your game doesn't use the desktop compositor's animations. Fine to do for taste; don't expect frames.

name: MMCSS SystemResponsiveness=0 / GPU Priority 8
what: Registry edits to multimedia scheduler weighting.
why: Trivial to apply, no measurable effect on modern Windows. The classic 'looks technical, does nothing' tweak.

name: Win32PrioritySeparation foreground boost
what: Registry value tuning foreground/background CPU quantum weighting.
why: Endlessly recycled in tweak guides with magic hex values; modern schedulers already prioritize the foreground. No measured benefit in controlled testing.

name: Forcing 0.5 ms global timer resolution
what: Forces Windows' interrupt timer to its finest interval system-wide.
why: This one does change things you can measure — just not reliably for the better, which is why it isn't a free win. A minority of systems get slightly steadier lows, some get worse, many see no change, and it raises idle power draw the whole time the timer is pinned; on a few specific older games it can also lift an odd frame-rate ceiling. Because the effect is inconsistent and comes with that cost, treat it as a measure-and-revert experiment, not a set-and-forget tweak: change it alone, watch your own numbers, and put it back unless it is clearly better on your machine.

name: Core unparking / force all cores active
what: Prevents Windows from parking idle CPU cores.
why: Modern Windows + modern CPUs already manage this well; forcing it mostly costs heat and can slightly HURT boost clocks. Same myth family as disabling C-States.

name: Disable C-States in BIOS
what: Stops CPU cores from entering low-power idle states.
why: The myth that actively backfires: modern boost algorithms USE the freed power budget from idle cores to clock active cores higher. Disabling C-States raises heat and LOWERS peak boost. Leave them on.

name: Disable / fix the pagefile
what: Turns off or hard-caps Windows' virtual memory file.
why: Refused. Games that commit more memory than your RAM will hard-crash with it off — '32 GB is enough' isn't how commit charge works. Leave it system-managed.

name: Disable Windows Defender
what: Turns off Windows' built-in antivirus for a supposed FPS gain.
why: Hard no. For the average rig the measured gain is a rounding error, and the cost is your only always-on protection — and some anti-cheats react badly to tampered security. If Defender's live scanning ever does cause stutter on one game (heavy disk I/O can trigger it), the right fix is a per-game folder exclusion, never killing your antivirus. Permanently blocklisted in Compy.

name: Disable Windows Update entirely
what: Kills the update service so Windows never patches.
why: Breaks Game Pass, anti-cheat compatibility, and security patching — and modern updates regularly fix game-relevant bugs and stability issues. Pause or schedule updates instead.

name: Disable CPU security mitigations (Spectre/Meltdown)
what: Turns off side-channel attack protections for a small CPU uplift.
why: For GAMING the gain is ~0–4% (the big numbers are servers); the cost is re-opening known, documented exploit classes. The FPS rounding error isn't worth it.

name: All-in-one debloat scripts / stripped ISOs
what: Scripts or custom Windows images that strip dozens of components at once.
why: The single biggest cause of mystery breakage: ten changes at once means no way to diagnose which one broke audio, anti-cheat, or updates. Some stripped images are irreversible. If you must debloat, change ONE thing at a time with an undo path.

name: Network 'mega-pack' tweaks (Nagle, RSS/RSC, netsh stacks)
what: Bundles of TCP/NIC registry and netsh changes promising lower ping.
why: Your ping is your route and your ISP, not a registry key. Single targeted changes (like Nagle, which Compy surfaces as advisory) have tiny effects in a few titles; the bundled packs mostly just break VoIP, VPNs, and smart-home apps.

name: IRQ priority / interrupt affinity hacks
what: Registry-deep manual control of which CPU cores service which device interrupts.
why: Negligible on modern, healthy systems and easy to break devices with. Only meaningful when diagnosing a specific DPC-latency problem with proper tools — which is what Compy's latency diagnostics (in Advanced) are for.

name: PBO / Curve Optimizer (AMD CPU tuning)
what: BIOS-level boost extension and per-core undervolting on Ryzen.
why: Real sustained-clock gains and cooler operation when dialed — but over-pushed values cause crashes that masquerade as 'random' instability for weeks. Advanced users only: small steps, hours of stress-testing, expect setbacks.

name: Toggling Secure Boot / CSM
what: Firmware settings controlling boot signature enforcement.
why: Not a performance setting at all — but anti-cheats (e.g. Vanguard) REQUIRE specific states, and toggling carelessly can leave a PC unbootable. Match your anti-cheat's requirement and know the recovery path before touching it.

name: Kernel tweak tools / DLL injectors / 'FPS unlocker' apps
what: Third-party tools that inject into game processes or load kernel components to 'optimize'.
why: Anti-cheat ban territory and a classic malware vector. If a tool touches game memory or ships a driver, assume it can cost you your account. Compy never injects — that's a design law, not a setting.

name: Keeping GPU drivers current
what: Installing current GPU drivers from AMD/NVIDIA (not auto-tools).
why: New titles regularly gain real performance from launch drivers. Get them from the vendor directly; use DDU for a clean reinstall only when something's actually wrong. Compy tracks your driver age and tells you when it's stale.

name: Registry "aim" tweaks
what: Registry edits, magic config files, and "pro settings" packs sold as sharpening your aim — steadier, snappier, more accurate.
why: No registry key aims for you. Aim is muscle memory plus how fast your input reaches the game — and the input half is set by things you can actually measure: raw input on, mouse acceleration off, a high and stable polling rate, low input latency, and steady frametimes. Compy already checks those. Everything past them that's sold as an "aim" fix changes nothing you can test. Put the time into an aim trainer, not regedit.

name: Disabling SMT / Hyper-Threading for gaming
what: Turning off your CPU's second thread per core (Hyper-Threading on Intel, SMT on AMD) in BIOS, on the theory that fewer, 'cleaner' threads game better.
why: On almost any modern 6-plus-core CPU this is a step backwards or a wash — you hand the game fewer threads to spread across and leave background work fighting it for what's left. The idea comes from ancient quad-cores that genuinely choked on thread count, a problem today's CPUs don't have. There is one honest exception: a narrow set of specific, heavily CPU-bound titles has measured a small gain with it off — so it isn't literally nothing everywhere, but that's the rare case, not the rule, and you'd be giving up thread headroom in everything else to chase it. Don't assume either way: change the one thing and watch your own 1% low. Compy never touches BIOS core settings.

name: NVIDIA "Prefer Maximum Performance" power mode
what: An NVIDIA Control Panel setting that pins the GPU at high clocks instead of letting it drop them when it thinks it's idle.
why: Real, but narrow. In a light esports title that never fully loads the card, the GPU can down-clock mid-match and add a little latency or a micro-stutter — locking clocks high stops that. In anything that actually loads the GPU it's already boosting, so this just burns a few extra watts and degrees for nothing. Worth a try on competitive titles, pointless elsewhere — set it per-game, not globally, and measure your 1% low before and after.

name: Pinning a game to specific CPU cores (affinity)
what: Hand-assigning a game to a hand-picked set of CPU cores in Task Manager or a tool like Process Lasso, on the theory you're keeping it off the 'busy' ones.
why: The Windows scheduler already places game threads better than a fixed list can, and it adapts as load shifts — a manual pin can't. At best it does nothing; at worst it starves the game of cores or, on a multi-die AMD chip, forces threads across the slow cross-die boundary you were trying to avoid. The thing that genuinely helps those chips is a one-complex setting, and Compy surfaces that as a measured, reversible suggestion — not a blanket affinity hack.

name: Disable memory compression
what: Turns off Windows' in-RAM compression of idle memory pages (Disable-MMAgent -mc).
why: Sold as cutting CPU overhead, but the overhead is tiny and the cost is real: under memory pressure cold pages go to disk instead of staying compressed in RAM — slower exactly when you're squeezed (game + browser + voice chat). Stock (on) is the right call on almost every rig; Compy's Past Tweaks check flags this when an old guide left it off.

name: Game booster apps (Razer Cortex etc.)
what: All-in-one 'booster' apps that promise FPS by closing background apps and 'optimizing' RAM or CPU when a game launches.
why: The one real thing they do — closing background apps — is free to do yourself, and Windows already deprioritizes background work while a game has focus. The 'RAM optimization' half is the standby-purge placebo, and the booster itself stays resident, sometimes with its own overlay on top. On a healthy rig there's nothing measurable left for it to add.

name: RAM cleaners / standby-list purgers (ISLC)
what: Utilities that 'free' RAM by purging Windows' standby list or trimming process memory on a timer.
why: Free RAM is wasted RAM: the standby list IS your file cache, and purging it throws away data Windows would have reused instantly — the next read comes from disk instead. The 2018-era standby-list stutter these tools were built around is something modern Windows memory management handles for most rigs now; today the falling 'in use' number mostly just looks satisfying while cold loads get slower.

name: Turning off hardware acceleration in Discord / Chrome
what: Disabling GPU ('hardware') acceleration in background apps like Discord or your browser to 'free the GPU' for games.
why: It moves those apps' rendering onto the CPU — the resource games are more often short on while the GPU is busy. A chat window costs the GPU next to nothing, and modern GPUs juggle apps fine. The toggle exists as a workaround for broken drivers, not a performance lever; flipping it 'for FPS' usually trades nothing gained for choppier app windows and a bit more CPU load.

name: Changing DNS for lower ping
what: Switching to a third-party 'gaming DNS' expecting lower in-game latency.
why: DNS answers one question — which IP a name points to — and it's asked when you connect, not while you play. Once you're in a match, packets flow straight to that IP; DNS isn't in the path anymore, so it can't lower ping. A faster resolver can shave a moment off page loads and server-list lookups, which is real — but it isn't in-game latency.

name: Running games as administrator for FPS
what: Launching a game with 'Run as administrator' expecting Windows to give it more CPU or GPU.
why: Administrator rights change what a program is ALLOWED to touch, not how fast it runs — an elevated game gets the same cores, the same scheduling, the same GPU time as a normal one, so there's no frame to gain. It's a legitimate troubleshooting step for a specific failure (a launcher that can't write its own folder, an anti-cheat driver that needs an elevated install) — use it to fix THAT, then go back. Leaving it on permanently hands every mod, overlay, and script the game loads the keys to your whole system, for a gain of exactly nothing.

name: Setting a game to High priority in Task Manager
what: Raising a game's CPU priority to High — or Realtime — in Task Manager so Windows favors it over everything else.
why: Priority only decides who wins when threads are FIGHTING for a core, and on a healthy rig running one game, nothing is fighting — Windows already favors the window you're playing in, so High changes nothing you can measure. Realtime is worse than nothing: it lets the game starve the system threads that feed it, which surfaces as crackling audio and stutters you didn't have before. And the setting dies with the process, so the ritual silently resets every launch. If something heavy genuinely competes with your game, the honest fix is closing it — and measuring the difference.

name: Defragging an SSD for speed
what: Running a full defragmenter pass on an SSD the way you would on an old hard drive.
why: Defrag fixes a mechanical problem: a spinning drive's read head physically traveling between scattered pieces of a file. An SSD has no moving parts and reads scattered pieces as fast as neat ones, so there is no speed to win back — but a full defrag pass still burns through write cycles, the thing an SSD has a finite budget of. Windows already knows the difference: its built-in Optimize Drives mainly gives an SSD a TRIM pass (a housekeeping hint that marks deleted space reusable), and only runs an occasional light defrag when System Restore is enabled — never the heavy, write-burning full pass a third-party defragmenter forces. Leave the built-in schedule alone and skip the third-party defragmenters.

name: GPU overclocking for FPS
what: Pushing your graphics card's core and memory clocks past stock with a tool like MSI Afterburner.
why: The gains are real but small — a stable overclock typically buys a few percent — and the cost of overshooting is weeks of 'random' crashes that look like driver bugs, game bugs, anything but the slider you moved last month. If you go in, go like a tester: one small step at a time, a stress run and a measured before/after per step, and write down what you changed so you can walk it back. Undervolting is the calmer cousin — often the same performance, cooler and quieter. Compy never overclocks anything; it can tell you whether your GPU is even the limiter first, so you know if there's anything here for you at all.

name: Reinstalling Windows every few months for FPS
what: Wiping and reinstalling Windows on a schedule, on the theory that an install 'wears out' and quietly eats FPS.
why: A genuinely rotted install — years of leftover services, startup hooks, and half-removed 'optimizers' — can measurably improve from a wipe, which is why the ritual has believers. But the reinstall isn't what helped; removing the rot was, and on a maintained PC there's nothing to remove. As a schedule, it costs you a weekend of reinstalling everything for frames that don't move. Compy's Check looks for the actual rot — leftover tweak debris, startup load — so you can see whether there's anything a wipe would even fix before you burn the weekend.

name: Forcing exclusive fullscreen for FPS
what: Always picking exclusive fullscreen over borderless, on the old rule that borderless costs FPS and adds lag.
why: That rule was true a decade ago. On Windows 10 and 11, a borderless game with nothing covering it gets handed the display almost as directly as exclusive mode ever did — the same frames, plus instant alt-tab and overlays that keep working. The one honest caveat is latency: exclusive fullscreen bypasses the desktop compositor, so at the competitive tier it can still shave a small, measurable slice of input lag — meaningful if you count every millisecond, invisible to most players. Either way it's measurable: play a session in each and compare, which is exactly the before/after Compy can time for you. Pick by measurement, not by 2014's rule.

name: Running MSI Afterburner / an overlay to boost FPS
what: The belief that running a monitoring tool like MSI Afterburner or RivaTuner — or its on-screen overlay — makes a game run faster.
why: A gauge reads the engine; it does not drive the car. Afterburner and RTSS measure framerate, temps, and usage — and measuring changes nothing about how many frames your GPU draws. The on-screen overlay actually costs a sliver of performance to render each frame (usually a fraction of a percent, more if you stack heavy graphs). The real worth of these tools is information — spotting a thermal or VRAM wall you can then act on. As a frame booster, there is nothing to measure.

name: Overclocking your monitor for more FPS
what: Pushing a monitor past its rated refresh rate (say 60 to 75 Hz) expecting the game to start producing more frames.
why: Refresh rate is the ceiling on frames you can SEE, not the number your GPU MAKES. Raising it lets a fast GPU show more of the frames it is already rendering — a real smoothness and latency win when your FPS was above the old refresh — but it adds zero frames on a GPU that was already the limit. A monitor overclock can also fail quietly: above a certain rate the panel may drop or repeat frames, so a '75 Hz' that is not showing 75 distinct frames is worse than an honest 60. Run a frame-skipping test before you trust it.

name: Closing every background app for more FPS
what: Manually shutting every background program — browser, Discord, wallpaper app — before a game, expecting a meaningful FPS jump.
why: On a modern multi-core PC with RAM to spare, idle apps sit there using almost nothing, so closing them frees memory and a few percent of one core the game was not waiting on. The exception is real: an app actively WORKING — a browser tab playing video, a cloud sync hammering the disk, a stream encoder — can steal a core or saturate your RAM and VRAM. Close THAT one and you will see it. Closing everything 'just in case' mostly buys you a tidier taskbar. The honest move is to watch usage and close only what is actually busy.

name: Disabling audio enhancements for FPS
what: Switching off Windows audio enhancements or spatial sound to free up performance for higher frames.
why: Audio processing runs on a tiny slice of CPU that has nothing to do with the GPU drawing frames — turning it off is a rounding error no frame counter will show. There IS a legitimate reason to toggle audio enhancements: they can cause crackling, echo, or delay in your SOUND, and turning them off fixes that. Do it for the audio. Do not expect frames from it.

name: Lowering render scale / resolution for FPS
what: Dropping the resolution a game RENDERS at — the output resolution, or an in-game 'render scale' / 'resolution scale' slider set below 100%.
why: This is the most reliable FPS lever there is, and the honest counterpoint to every placebo registry tweak: frames cost pixels, so rendering fewer pixels makes more frames, every time, on every GPU. Going from 1440p to 1080p, or render scale 100% to 80%, gives a large and measurable jump whenever you are GPU-limited. The trade is sharpness. Modern upscalers (DLSS / FSR / XeSS) are the smart version — they render low and reconstruct detail so you keep most of the image — but even a plain resolution drop works. When a tweak promises free frames at no visual cost, doubt it; this one is honest about the cost and actually delivers the frames.

name: Turning off HDR for more FPS
what: Switching HDR off in Windows or in-game to claw back frames.
why: HDR widens the range of brightness and color the display shows — it is mostly more information per pixel, not more pixels, so on a modern GPU the extra work is a sliver, often too small for any frame counter to show. It does use a little more video memory (VRAM), and a game with badly tuned HDR can look washed-out or dim — and THAT is the honest reason to toggle it: image quality, not performance. If your frame number does not move, it did not help. Turn HDR off because you prefer how the standard (SDR) image looks, or because a game's HDR is mis-calibrated — not for frames.

name: Disabling mouse acceleration for FPS
what: Turning off mouse acceleration — Windows 'Enhance pointer precision', or an in-game acceleration setting — to gain frames.
why: Mouse acceleration changes how far your crosshair travels based on how FAST you move the mouse — it shapes how aiming feels and touches nothing the GPU does to draw a frame, so no frame counter will move. There is a strong reason to turn it off anyway: with acceleration on, the same hand motion lands a different distance depending on speed, so your muscle memory never settles; off gives you a consistent 1-to-1 feel. That is an aim-consistency win, not an FPS win. Do it for control, and don't expect frames.

name: Running RAM in dual-channel (two sticks)
what: Using two matched memory sticks so RAM runs in dual-channel, instead of a single stick running in single-channel.
why: This is a real, measurable FPS lever — the kind a registry tweak only pretends to be. Two channels roughly double how fast the CPU can move data in and out of memory, and games lean on that bandwidth, especially when the CPU is the limit and dramatically on laptops and APUs that borrow system memory for graphics. A single stick can cost double-digit percentages of average FPS and hurt your 1% lows even more, so the frames stutter. Match a second stick to your first (same capacity and speed), seat them in the slots your motherboard manual marks for dual-channel, and switch on the rated speed profile (XMP/EXPO). The cost is one stick of RAM; the gain shows up on the frame counter.

name: Disabling Nagle's algorithm for lower lag
what: Registry edits (TcpAckFrequency / TCPNoDelay) that switch off Nagle's algorithm — the thing that batches tiny network packets — to 'reduce lag.'
why: Nagle's algorithm groups small packets together to be efficient, which in theory could add a few milliseconds before your input goes out. But it has nothing to do with FPS — your GPU draws frames locally — and for online lag the tweak almost never matters: most competitive games run on UDP, which Nagle does not touch at all, and the ones on TCP usually turn Nagle off themselves per-connection. So the registry edit is overridden or irrelevant for the games people apply it to. If one specific older TCP game documents it, fine; otherwise it is a tweak that sounds technical and changes nothing you will feel.

name: Disabling Fast Startup for FPS
what: Turning off Windows 'Fast Startup' (hybrid shutdown) expecting smoother or faster games.
why: Fast Startup makes your PC boot quicker by saving part of Windows to disk on shutdown instead of fully closing it. That is a boot-time feature — it does nothing to how many frames a game draws once you are in it. There IS an honest reason some people disable it: because it does not fully reset the system, a flaky driver or device state can carry across reboots, so turning it off (or doing a full 'Restart' instead of 'Shut down') is a real troubleshooting step. Do it to get a truly clean boot, not for frames.

name: Switching to Ethernet for more FPS
what: Plugging in an Ethernet cable instead of Wi-Fi expecting a higher frame rate.
why: Your network carries your inputs to the game server and back — that is ping and latency, not frames. The frames themselves are drawn by your GPU on your own PC, with the network nowhere in that loop, so your FPS counter will not move. Here is the honest part: for ONLINE games, wired Ethernet genuinely is better — lower, steadier ping and far fewer lag spikes than Wi-Fi — which makes the game FEEL more responsive even at the same FPS. Use Ethernet for the connection quality; just do not expect the frame counter to climb.

name: Turning off background recording (Instant Replay) for FPS
what: Switching off always-on background capture — NVIDIA Instant Replay / Shadowplay, AMD's equivalent, or Game Bar's background recording — to free up performance.
why: This one is real, but small and honest. Background recording constantly encodes your gameplay using the GPU's built-in video encoder, and that work is not free — it is typically a low single-digit percentage of your frames on a modern card, more on an older or already-maxed-out GPU, or at a high capture resolution and bitrate. So if you are GPU-limited and not using the clips, turning it off gives back a small, measurable slice of FPS. If you love grabbing highlights, the cost is usually worth it — keep it on. Measure your own before and after rather than assuming; that is the only honest way to know your number.

name: Setting Windows to your monitor's full refresh rate
what: Making sure Windows is actually driving your monitor at its rated refresh rate (say 144Hz or 165Hz), not silently running it at 60Hz.
why: This is the most common 'my expensive monitor feels like 60fps' fix there is, and it is genuinely real. Windows often defaults a high-refresh monitor to 60Hz — especially after a new cable, a driver update, or adding a second display — so the panel can only SHOW 60 frames a second no matter how many your GPU draws. Set it in Settings → System → Display → Advanced display, and choose your monitor's top refresh rate. The change is instant, free, and fully reversible. If your monitor was stuck at 60Hz, this is the single biggest smoothness upgrade you can make without spending a cent — your GPU was already making the frames; the screen just was not showing them.

name: Buying a bigger power supply for more FPS
what: Upgrading to a higher-wattage power supply expecting more frames.
why: A power supply's job is to deliver enough clean, stable power — not to make your GPU faster. Once it comfortably covers what your parts draw, adding more watts changes nothing your frame counter will see. There IS a real failure mode at the other end: a power supply that is too small, failing, or low-quality can cause crashes, shutdowns, or the GPU pulling back under load — but the fix there is an ADEQUATE, good-quality unit, not just a bigger number. Size it to your hardware with a little headroom and move on; wattage past that is money the frame counter will not thank you for.

name: Running a registry cleaner for FPS
what: Using a 'registry cleaner' / 'registry optimizer' tool that promises faster games by deleting old registry entries.
why: The Windows registry is a settings database, not a performance bottleneck — a few thousand stale entries cost you nothing measurable, and no game reads them while it is drawing frames. So the upside is zero. The downside is real: these tools delete entries by guesswork, and a wrong delete can break an app, a driver, or Windows itself — sometimes days later, once you have forgotten you ran it. That is why this is graded risky, not just placebo: no frames to gain, and a genuine chance of a mess to clean up. If something specific is broken, fix THAT; do not let a tool sweep the whole registry hoping for speed.

name: Chasing a lower monitor response time for FPS
what: Buying or tuning for a lower monitor response time (the '1ms' number) expecting a higher frame rate.
why: Response time measures how fast a single pixel changes color — it affects motion clarity and ghosting (the smear behind fast-moving objects), not how many frames your GPU produces. A '1ms' panel and a '4ms' panel at the same refresh rate give you the exact same FPS. It is a real spec worth caring about for crispness in fast games, but it is not a frame-rate lever — and the marketing '1ms' figures are often measured generously anyway. Want more frames? Look at refresh rate, resolution, and settings, not the response-time sticker.

name: Buying more RAM for more FPS
what: Adding more system memory — 16→32GB, or 32→64GB — expecting the frame rate to climb.
why: Games need ENOUGH memory, not endless memory. Once you comfortably cover what the game and Windows use, extra capacity just sits there — a 64GB kit draws the same frames as a 32GB one in today's games. The real failure mode is the opposite: if you are actually short (8GB on a modern game, or 16GB with a browser full of tabs and a game that wants more), the system spills onto the slow drive and you get stutter and ugly 1% lows — and THEN adding RAM genuinely helps. So check whether you are actually running out before you buy. For most people on 16–32GB the frames are already all there; capacity past 'enough' is a placebo. Memory SPEED and running in dual-channel are the levers that do move frames — that is a different thing.

name: Needing PCIe 4.0/5.0 for more FPS
what: Believing your graphics card needs a newer PCIe slot version (4.0 or 5.0) to hit higher frame rates.
why: A modern graphics card running in a full-width (x16) PCIe 3.0 slot loses almost nothing versus 4.0 — usually low single digits, often inside the margin of error. Games do not shovel enough data across that link for the version to matter at x16. Where it CAN bite is narrow cases: a card wired for only four lanes (some budget GPUs), or a slot dropped to x8/x4 because an M.2 drive or a second card is sharing the lanes — there a newer PCIe gen recovers real frames. So check how many lanes your card actually gets before worrying about the version. For the typical 'GPU in the top x16 slot' setup, PCIe gen is not your frame-rate lever.

name: Turning down the heaviest graphics settings
what: Dropping the GPU-heavy in-game settings — ray tracing, shadows, reflections, volumetric fog, view distance — to gain frames.
why: After resolution, this is the most reliable FPS lever there is, and it is honest about the trade: these settings cost real GPU work, so turning the few heaviest ones down buys real, measurable frames. The trick is they are not equal — ray tracing, shadow quality, and volumetric/cloud effects are usually the expensive ones, while textures (if you have the video memory for them) and anisotropic filtering are nearly free and worth keeping. Drop the top two or three offenders from Ultra to High/Medium and you often keep most of the look for a big chunk of the frames. Use the game's built-in benchmark to see which setting moves YOUR number, instead of nuking everything to Low and playing an ugly game for frames you did not need.

name: Disabling integrated graphics for more FPS
what: Disabling the CPU's built-in (integrated) graphics in Device Manager or the BIOS, expecting your dedicated card to run faster.
why: Your dedicated graphics card is already doing all the rendering — the integrated GPU sits idle while you game and costs you no frames to leave on. Turning it off does nothing for FPS, and it can actually cost you: the integrated GPU powers some video-encoding (handy for recording without touching the game), drives extra display outputs, and is a lifesaver for troubleshooting if the dedicated card ever fails. Leave it enabled. If a game is somehow rendering on the integrated GPU by mistake, the fix is to set that GAME to use the dedicated card (Windows Graphics settings), not to disable half your hardware.

name: Buying a pricier motherboard for more FPS
what: Spending more on a higher-end motherboard expecting the games to run at a higher frame rate.
why: A motherboard does not render frames — it connects the parts that do. Two boards with the same CPU, RAM, and GPU produce the same FPS. What a better board actually buys is around the edges: stronger power delivery for a heavy overclock, more/faster M.2 and USB, better Wi-Fi or networking, and support for higher memory speeds — and THAT last one is the only part that touches frames, by letting your RAM run its rated profile. So buy the board for the features and the memory support you need, not for frames. The cheap board with the same RAM speed games exactly as fast.

name: Updating your BIOS for more FPS
what: Flashing a motherboard BIOS update expecting a direct jump in frame rate.
why: A BIOS update almost never changes raw FPS on its own — it is firmware for the board, not a performance switch. What it CAN do is real but indirect: on AMD especially, a newer BIOS (AGESA) can unlock better, more stable memory support, so a RAM kit that would not run its rated speed before now can — and faster, stable memory genuinely helps frames. It also fixes stability bugs and adds support for newer CPUs. So update your BIOS for stability, memory compatibility, or a CPU upgrade — good reasons — but treat any frame gain as a side effect of better memory, not the update itself. And flash carefully: a botched BIOS update is one of the few ways to actually brick a board.

name: Manually overclocking your CPU for more FPS
what: Pushing your CPU past stock with a manual all-core overclock to gain frames in games.
why: Modern CPUs already boost themselves hard, and games mostly lean on one or two fast cores — so a manual all-core overclock often LOWERS the single-core boost a game wants while raising heat and the chance of random crashes, for little or no gaming gain. That is why this is graded risky: real downside, thin upside. The smart, calmer path on a modern chip is the opposite — undervolting or a curve optimizer (PBO on AMD) to hold higher boost clocks cooler, which Compy points you to as a measured, reversible tune. If you do chase a manual overclock anyway, go like a tester: one small step, a stress run, a measured before and after — and keep stock settings written down so you can walk it back.

name: Putting a game on an SSD for more FPS
what: Moving a game from a hard drive to an SSD (or to a faster NVMe SSD) expecting a higher frame rate.
why: Once a game is loaded and running, the frames come from your GPU and CPU — the drive is barely in the loop, so your average FPS looks the same on a hard drive, a SATA SSD, or a fast NVMe drive. What an SSD genuinely transforms is everything AROUND the frame rate: far shorter load times, and much less of the hitching and texture pop-in you get when a fast-moving game streams data off a slow hard drive — so an SSD can smooth your 1% lows and stutters even when the average number does not move. Use an SSD (it is one of the best feel upgrades there is); just file it under load times and smoothness, not raw FPS. Jumping from a good SATA SSD to a faster NVMe one does almost nothing for games today.

name: Plugging in your laptop for more FPS
what: Gaming with the charger plugged in instead of on battery — and making sure Windows is not in a battery-saver power mode.
why: On a laptop this is one of the biggest free FPS swings there is, and it is completely real. Running on battery, the laptop deliberately throttles the CPU and GPU hard to save power and heat — you can lose a third or more of your frames versus plugged in. Plug in the charger, set Windows to its 'Best performance' power mode, and in the laptop maker's app (like Armoury Crate or Lenovo Vantage) pick the performance or turbo profile. The frames come back instantly, and you can switch it all back the moment you unplug. If your laptop still feels slow while plugged in, that is a separate thing — usually heat (clean the vents, raise the back for airflow) or the game running on the integrated GPU instead of the dedicated one.

name: Switching between Windows 11 and 10 for FPS
what: Switching from Windows 11 to 10 (or back) expecting a meaningful frame-rate change.
why: For frame rate the two are close to a wash today — early Windows 11 had a few gaming regressions, but those were patched, and any difference now is small enough to vanish in normal run-to-run variation. There ARE real reasons to prefer one: Windows 11 schedules work better on newer hybrid CPUs (the performance/efficiency-core chips) and adds Auto HDR and DirectStorage, while some people just prefer 10's layout — and Windows 10 is heading out of support, which matters more for security than for frames. So choose your version for features, hardware, and support, not for FPS. Reinstalling your whole OS to chase frames is a lot of work for a difference you will not reliably measure.

name: Raising your mouse DPI for more FPS
what: Cranking up your mouse's DPI (sensitivity) expecting a higher or smoother frame rate.
why: DPI sets how far the aim moves per inch of mouse travel — it is a sensitivity setting, and it has nothing to do with how many frames your GPU draws. A 400-DPI mouse and a 26,000-DPI mouse give you the exact same FPS. What DPI affects is your AIM: too high and it is twitchy, too low and you run out of mousepad. Pick a DPI (most pros sit in the 400–1600 range) plus an in-game sensitivity that lets you do a comfortable 180 with about a forearm's sweep, and leave it. The thing on a mouse that CAN actually touch performance — a very high polling rate — is a different setting, and one that tends to cost a sliver of FPS rather than add it.
